claim: Did you know… a Berlin horse could do arithmetic by tapping its hoof?

studies.finding: Systematic tests showed the horse answered by reading involuntary head and body movements of whoever asked, and failed when it could not see them.
studies.verdict: Horse was real and skilled; the skill was reading people, not arithmetic.

claim: Did you know… cattle worldwide tend to graze facing north or south?

studies.finding: Satellite images of thousands of cattle, plus field observations of cattle and deer, showed bodies aligned roughly north-south, tracking magnetic rather than geographic north.
studies.verdict: Provocative; independent groups did not reproduce it from similar images.

studies.cite: Hert et al. (2011), J Comp Physiol A
studies.finding: Using Google satellite photos of 3,412 cattle in European herds, two independent groups found no alignment with geomagnetic field lines.
studies.verdict: Failure to reproduce, with image quality and observer bias suggested as causes.

studies.cite: Begall et al. (2011), J Comp Physiol A
studies.finding: Reanalysis of the Hert data, after discarding unusable images, found a north-south axis, stronger in lying cattle.
studies.verdict: Authors of the original claim rebutting; no neutral resolution.

claim: Did you know… dogs prefer to face north or south when they defecate?

studies.cite: Hart et al. (2013), Frontiers in Zoology
studies.finding: In 70 dogs, body axis during excretion lined up north-south, but only when the magnetic field was calm.
studies.verdict: Observational and post hoc condition; later independent attempt did not reproduce it.

studies.finding: Repeating a later park-based dog study at five Lyon parks, the authors measured dog orientation during urination and defecation.
studies.verdict: No magnetic alignment found; dogs oriented to park layout instead.

claim: Did you know… a dog's guilty look is a response to scolding, not guilt?

studies.finding: In 14 dogs, guilty-look behaviours followed the owner's scolding, whether or not the dog had actually eaten the forbidden treat.
studies.verdict: Result stands; it does not rule out guilt, only finds no evidence of it.

claim: Did you know… a chimpanzee learned sign language well enough to build sentences?

studies.finding: Analysis of over 19,000 multi-sign utterances by the chimpanzee Nim found most were prompted by his teacher's preceding signs, with frequent interruptions.
studies.verdict: Project's own reanalysis: no evidence of grammar; ape-language claims largely abandoned.

claim: Did you know… fish feel pain much as mammals do?

studies.cite: Sneddon et al. (2003), Proc R Soc B
studies.finding: Rainbow trout had nociceptors on the head, and acid applied to the lips changed breathing rate, delayed feeding and produced unusual behaviour.
studies.verdict: Nociception established; whether it is felt as pain remains disputed.

studies.finding: Argued that fish lack the cortex-like structure and connectivity that human pain experience depends on, so behaviour does not show pain.
studies.verdict: Contested in published commentaries; no consensus reached.

claim: Did you know… a parasite makes rats attracted to the smell of cats?

studies.cite: Berdoy et al. (2000), Proc R Soc B
studies.finding: Rats infected with Toxoplasma gondii lost their usual avoidance of cat-scented areas, and some were drawn to them.
studies.verdict: Influential, but later experiments gave inconsistent results across labs.

studies.finding: Infection turned rodents' innate aversion to feline odour into attraction, without impairing learned fear or other tests.
studies.verdict: Supports a specific effect in the original design.

studies.finding: Review of rodent experiments on Toxoplasma and behaviour found no consistent direction or size of effects across studies.
studies.verdict: Evidence mixed; strain, species and test methods differ.

claim: Did you know… pigeons fed at random develop superstitions?

studies.finding: Pigeons given food at fixed intervals regardless of behaviour developed repeated rituals in six of eight birds, read as accidental reinforcement.
studies.verdict: Observation real; the accidental-reinforcement explanation was challenged.

studies.finding: A reexamination of the superstition experiment, observing pigeons' behaviour in detail between food deliveries.
studies.verdict: Reinterpreted as food-timed, species-typical behaviour, not learned superstition.

claim: Did you know… wild crows remember human faces and pass the grudge on?

studies.cite: Cornell et al. (2012), Proc R Soc B
studies.finding: Crows trapped by a masked person scolded that mask later, and so did crows never captured, including young taught by parents.
studies.verdict: Field result; learning spread socially across years and kilometres.

studies.finding: Brain imaging of wild crows showed threatening faces activated fear-related regions, and caring faces activated motivation regions.
studies.verdict: Neural evidence consistent with face recognition.

claim: Did you know… rats laugh when tickled?

studies.finding: Rats emit ultrasonic 50-kHz chirps during play and tickling, proposed as a primitive form of laughter.
studies.verdict: Framework later supported by neural recordings.

studies.finding: Tickled rats produced laughter-calls and joy jumps, and somatosensory cortex cells responded to tickling and play.
studies.verdict: Brain activity tracked ticklishness; anxiety suppressed both.
